newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Oil companies best hope for remote Australian island.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil companies best hope for remote Australian island.

text.p: For three decades this pristine dot in the Indian Ocean, where amber spinifex weed grows rampant and pillar-like "termite tents" rise six feet (two metres) high, has enjoyed an unlikely protector.
A consortium of oil companies has made Barrow Island into Australia's largest on-shore oil field, yet allowed its wildlife to flourish.

But the crude deposits are becoming harder to get at and environmentalists now fear that when the oil companies eventually leave the island, there will be nothing to discourage hordes of rampaging tourists.
"Oil companies are not the problem, people are the problem," Harry Butler, a leading environmentalist and the island's official warden, told Reuters on a recent visit.

The sole inhabitants of Barrow Island are some 200 oil workers, employed by the West Australia Petroleum (Wapet) consortium, which has extracted crude from the remote oil patch located 56 km (34 miles) off mainland northwest Australia since the 1960s.
There are no fixed structures on the island apart from a workers' camp and canteen. A single road around the island is unpaved.

Legions of hamster-like bandicoots roam free, as do thousands of wallabies and other indigenous creatures. During their time off, the workers are free to do as they please. Some fish or surf off the island's remarkably unspoilt coastline or "go walkabout", wandering over rows of soft hills.
The work roster is two weeks on, two weeks off. Transport to and from the island is by light airplane.
However, the once-rich crude deposits are drying up and there is talk of introducing tourism if the oil companies abandon the island.
The oil industry has been good to Barrow Island, said Butler, known to millions of Australians for crusading environmental televison programmes in the 1960s and 1970s.
Less than five percent of the 234 square-kilometre (90 square-mile) island has been disturbed by oil drilling, he said.

His greatest concern is that the oil pumps connected by pipelines running across the spinifex and termite tents -- erected by an ever-growing army of white ants -- will give way to townhouses and fishing piers, threatening the delicate eco-system of the island.
"Wapet has been very good to this little place because they realise it's so special to Australia," said Butler.
Relations between Butler and the oil companies were not always so friendly. When Wapet first arrived on the island Butler said he had his reservations.
"The idea of oil companies coming to Barrow Island was a bit worrying," Butler said. "This place doesn't take well to outsiders."
Barrow Island has been good to Wapet, too. Around 270 million barrels of oil have been recovered from the island so far and there's plenty more.
But Wapet, comprising subsidiaries of Texaco, Chevron and Caltex, has been forced to dig deeper for oil as the more shallow reserves are depleted, said Cliff Leggoe, a spokesman for the consortium.
In about 15 years it may be uneconomic to continue drilling for oil on the island, which has the Western Australia state government thinking about opening it up to tourism.
The consortium this week announced dramatic job cutbacks because of declining oil production in Western Australia state, including on Barrow Island.
"No one wants to leave Barrow Island, but we've got to find more oil," said Wapet spokesman Leggoe.
